Pregnancy

Back pain and labour: signs, causes and relief

Updated: October 19, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Backache is common in pregnancy and can also accompany labour. It cannot tell you on its own whether birth is approaching. Notice changes from your usual symptoms, contractions, fluid leakage, bleeding and your baby’s movements, and contact your maternity team when you are unsure. Strong or persistent pain deserves assessment rather than being dismissed as an inevitable part of birth.

Does back pain mean labour has started?

Labour may bring a low backache or heavy aching sensation, sometimes with tightening of the abdomen. Contractions often become stronger, longer and closer together. However, some people mainly notice back pain, and the absence of a familiar contraction pattern does not exclude labour.

A mucus ‘show’ or the baby settling lower in the pelvis may occur before birth, but neither predicts the day. Waters may break before or during labour. A change with rest or movement can be useful information for your team, but is not a home test that confirms or rules out labour.

Why pregnancy itself can cause backache

Hormonal changes soften supporting ligaments, while the growing uterus, changing balance and extra load affect muscles and joints. Abdominal muscles also stretch. These changes can contribute to pain at different stages of pregnancy, separately from labour.

Muscle strain, pelvic girdle pain and existing spinal problems can also matter. Fever, burning urination or pain in the side under the ribs needs prompt medical advice because infection is another possibility. Tell your team about new or changing pain rather than assuming it has the same cause as an earlier ache.

What back labour can feel like

Back labour describes prominent lower-back pain during labour. It can intensify with contractions and sometimes remain between them. Experiences vary; a fixed percentage does not predict whether it will happen to you or how much relief you will need.

Ask for support and pain relief early if you are struggling. Severe pain that persists or worsens, including pain with little relief between contractions, needs immediate assessment; do not decide by yourself that it is simply back labour. Clinicians may check you, the baby and the contraction pattern to assess the cause.

Baby position, spinal conditions and body shape

Pressure from the baby’s head may contribute. An occiput-posterior position means the head is down with the face towards your abdomen; it can be associated with back pain. Pain alone cannot identify the position, and a head-down baby does not automatically cause back labour.

Tell your maternity and anaesthetic teams about scoliosis, previous spinal surgery or other back conditions so that positioning and pain relief can be planned. The normal increase in the lower-back curve during pregnancy is not automatically a spinal disease. A narrow waist does not establish that you will have severe labour pain, and pain is not a failure of posture or preparation.

When to contact your maternity team

Call immediately if you think your waters have broken, your baby moves less or differently than usual, or you have any vaginal bleeding during pregnancy. Before 37 weeks, unusual backache, period-like pains or tightenings need immediate maternity advice, even without a regular contraction pattern. Do not wait until morning or for home measures to work.

If you think labour is starting, call for guidance and follow your individual birth plan. Timing advice depends on your pregnancy, previous births, travel distance and local service. There is no single ten-minute interval or contraction duration that everyone should wait for. Tell the team the gestation, pain pattern, fluid or bleeding and movement changes; they will advise where and when to be assessed.

Symptoms needing emergency help

Seek emergency care for severe persistent or worsening back or abdominal pain, heavy bleeding, fainting or loss of consciousness, chest pain or breathing difficulty. If you think the baby is coming now and have a strong urge to push, call an ambulance. Do not drive yourself to emergency care; ask another person to drive or call an ambulance.

Back pain with new numbness around the genitals or anus, new loss of feeling in one or both legs, symptoms in both legs, difficulty passing urine or new loss of bladder or bowel control also needs emergency assessment. Do not attribute these signs to normal pregnancy or a known back condition. Fever or urinary symptoms with back pain needs urgent medical advice; tell the service that you are pregnant.

Movement and supported positions

After advice about your symptoms, try positions that feel comfortable and are safe for your situation: leaning forward onto a stable support, side-lying, kneeling or hands-and-knees. Gentle walking or changing position may help in early labour if you feel able. Stop if you become dizzy or pain increases.

A correctly sized stable birth ball or supported squat may suit some people, with help to avoid falls. Do not force a movement, use an unstable surface or assume a position will turn the baby. Monitoring, leg weakness, medicines or complications may change what is safe; ask the team before getting up after an epidural.

Warmth, massage and calming techniques

A comfortably warm shower or bath, or a wrapped warm pack on the back, may ease discomfort. Avoid overheating and burns. Ask about water use if your care plan or monitoring changes; suspected broken waters still needs an immediate call. A support person can offer gentle massage or counterpressure if you want it, stopping when touch is unwelcome.

Slow breathing, relaxation, music, meditation or learned hypnosis techniques may help you cope, but do not guarantee pain relief. Massage does not require essential oils; check any product with the maternity team and avoid irritants. These options can accompany medicines, and should never postpone assessment or a request for more effective relief.

Medicines and clinical pain-relief options

Discuss what is available, its benefits, side effects and your preferences. Options can include gas and air, selected opioid medicines, an epidural and, in some services, sterile-water injections given by a trained professional for back pain. You may change your mind about pain relief; you do not have to endure severe pain to follow an earlier plan.

Pain medicines do not all preserve alertness, muscle control or walking. An epidural may make legs heavy; staff must check strength and sensation and arrange appropriate assistance. Ask your clinician or pharmacist before self-medicating in pregnancy. Do not self-treat with ibuprofen or other NSAIDs, particularly from 20 weeks; do not stop prescribed low-dose aspirin without advice. If paracetamol is advised, follow the product instructions and avoid duplicate ingredients.

Can back labour be prevented?

Comfortable supported sitting, changing position, sensible lifting and activity adapted to your pregnancy may help ordinary backache. Bend your knees when lifting and avoid loads that strain you. A maternity physiotherapist can help with persistent symptoms and a plan suited to an existing spinal or pelvic problem.

These measures do not guarantee prevention of back labour. Neither a particular sitting rule, avoiding crossed legs nor perfect preparation ensures a certain baby position or painless birth. Keep a flexible support and pain-relief plan, and seek assessment for new symptoms rather than blaming yourself or trying harder through pain.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Agree on whom to call, transport and your individual labour-contact plan; report pain, gestation, movements, fluid and bleeding without waiting for a set clock pattern.

Discuss previous spinal problems, safe supported positions and available pain relief with your team; ask for reassessment if pain is not controlled.

Use comfort measures only when appropriate, check medicine and product safety, and act on warning signs before logging symptoms or trying another home measure.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can help you record pain patterns, contractions, questions and your maternity contact plan. It cannot confirm labour, identify the baby’s position, assess wellbeing or choose safe medicines. Warning signs require care rather than further tracking.

When to seek help

Call maternity care immediately for waters breaking, any pregnancy bleeding, changed baby movements or unusual backache/possible labour before 37 weeks. Seek emergency care for severe persistent or worsening pain, heavy bleeding, fainting or loss of consciousness, chest pain, breathing difficulty or new nerve/bladder/bowel symptoms. Call an ambulance for an imminent birth with a strong urge to push. Do not drive yourself in an emergency or wait for a bath, medicine or contraction timer. Check pregnancy medicines with a professional.

Evidence notes updated: October 19, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Backache can accompany labour, but pain or its response to rest cannot diagnose it.
  • Contact maternity care immediately for waters breaking, any pregnancy bleeding, movement changes or possible labour before 37 weeks.
  • Baby position and existing back problems may influence pain; waist size cannot predict your experience.
  • Supported movement, warmth and calming techniques can complement individual clinical pain relief.
  • Severe persistent pain, neurological or bladder/bowel changes and other emergency signs need immediate care.

Frequently asked questions

Can back pain be a sign of labour?

Yes, but backache alone cannot confirm labour. Tightenings, fluid leakage and other changes help the maternity team assess you. Call if you think labour has started or are unsure.

What causes back labour?

Pressure from the baby’s head can contribute, sometimes with an occiput-posterior position. Other muscle, pelvic or spinal factors may matter. Symptoms alone cannot identify the baby’s position or exclude another problem.

Does a narrow waist make labour back pain worse?

Waist size is not a reliable way to predict your pain. Tell your team about previous back conditions and ask for an individual plan; do not blame your body shape or preparation.

Should I go to hospital when my back starts hurting?

Contact maternity care for advice about new or changing pain. Call immediately for broken waters, bleeding, changed baby movements or possible labour before 37 weeks. Follow your personal plan rather than waiting for a universal contraction interval.

Does pain easing with rest rule out labour?

No. Symptoms can fluctuate and early labour varies. Do not use rest, hydration, a bath or a painkiller as a test that delays needed assessment.

What if I am not yet 37 weeks pregnant?

Unusual backache, period-like pain, tightenings or fluid leakage needs immediate contact with your maternity team. You do not need to wait for stronger or regularly timed contractions.

Can I choose medicines as well as comfort measures?

Yes. Discuss available options and their effects on alertness, movement and monitoring. Do not self-treat with NSAIDs in pregnancy or change prescribed medicines without advice; comfort measures do not replace assessment.

When should I get emergency help?

Severe persistent or worsening back or abdominal pain, heavy bleeding, fainting or loss of consciousness, chest pain or breathing difficulty require emergency care. New genital/anal numbness, new loss of feeling in one or both legs, symptoms in both legs or bladder/bowel changes also require emergency assessment. Call an ambulance for an imminent birth with a strong urge to push; do not drive yourself in an emergency.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
